Located at the centre of the Bab al-Mandab Strait,  Mayyun Island is a key monitoring point overlooking the vital maritime passage.

Two Yemeni sources also told Reuters that Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces had withdrawn from Perim Island.

The development came after Houthis seized the western coastal city of Mocha, forcing the government forces to retreat toward the south and the city of Dhubab.

The Sanaa-based Yemen Press Agency, citing field sources, said Houthi forces seized the al-Omari camp overlooking the strait.

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree was also reported as saying that navigation in the Red Sea was safe except for Saudi ships, suggesting the group now has control over the Strait of Mandeb.

Known as the "Gate of Tears" in Arabic, because of its history of shipwrecks, the strait sits at the southern tip of the Red Sea, connecting it with the Gulf of Aden in the Indian Ocean.

About 100 kilometres long and just 30 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, it separates Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula from Djibouti and Eritrea on the Horn of Africa.

With the Red Sea linking maritime trade between Europe and Asia, the strait is usually one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

Oil tankers and cargo ships use it to reach the Mediterranean via the Suez Canal, shortening journeys between Asia and Europe and North America by thousands of kilometres (miles).

In 2024, as the Houthis attacked Red Sea shipping during the Gaza war, Suez Canal traffic fell sharply and has yet to recover, according to IMF PortWatch data analysed by AFP.

Total transits dropped from 26,895 vessels in 2023, or 73.7 per day, to 14,498 in 2024 and 14,070 in 2025, AFP reported.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] UK's Charity Commission issues regulatory advice to Board of Deputies following ICJP complaint
item.description:
UK's Charity Commission issues regulatory advice to Board of Deputies following ICJP complaint

Submitted by MEE staff on Sat, 09/12/2026 - 05:37
The Board had accused organisers of staging the protest against Great Israeli Real Estate Event in London on ‘bogus grounds’
People from pro-Palestinian activist groups gather outside the Edgware United Synagogue, during a demonstration against the Great Israeli Real Estate Event, in London, on 14 June 2026. (Reuters)
Off

The UK’s Charity Commission has reminded a British charity funding the Board of Deputies of British Jews that risks arise when a charity ‘is, or perceived to be, closely associated with a company’, following a protest against a London real estate event that promoted properties in illegal Israeli settlements.

The regulatory guidance and advice to the trustees of the Board of Deputies Charitable Foundation, which also executes the activities of the Board of Deputies of British Jews (BDBJ), comes in response to a complaint filed by the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP). 

In a statement, ICJP said that the Board of Deputies of British Jews had claimed that a protest demonstration held outside Edgware United Synagogue, which hosted the Great Israeli Real Estate Event, was organised on “bogus grounds”.

The ICJP said that the Board made the accusations as it had relied on assurances from the event organisers that properties in the illegal settlements would not be marketed.

It characterised the protest as an attempt to “harass and intimidate members of the Jewish community”. 

But the organisers later apologised for including several properties in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem in their brochure. 

Exclusive: Illegal settlements promoted in London at Great Israeli Real Estate Event
Read More »

“ICJP’s complaint raised concerns about the failure to correct or withdraw the Board’s statements after evidence emerged substantiating the protesters’ concerns,” the statement said.

“It argued that the statements risked misrepresenting a protest against activities connected to Israel’s illegal settlement enterprise as an attack upon a synagogue or the Jewish community.” 

In its response, the charity regulator noted that the statements appeared to have been issued by The Board of Deputies of British Jews Limited, rather than the charitable foundation itself.

“Nevertheless, the Commission considered it appropriate to issue advice and guidance to the charity’s trustees under section 15(2) of the Charities Act 2011,” ICJP said.

“The Commission confirmed that it has reminded the charity’s trustees of the risks that arise where a charity ‘is, or is perceived to be, closely associated with a company, particularly in relation to public statements and communications.’” 

The Commission will retain the information ICJP provided and may take it into account in any future regulatory engagement with the charity, ICJP said. 

Shaima Dallali, ICJP’s legal researcher, said: “Palestinians are being driven from their land while that same land is marketed to buyers abroad, including in the UK. These are not ordinary property exhibitions. They are part of the economic infrastructure that sustains Israel’s unlawful occupation and settlement enterprise. Those who protested were challenging precisely the activity that the UK government is now moving to prohibit.”  

“The Board of Deputies must correct the public record,” Dallali said.

Charity Commission Criticism

In a statement to MEE on 13 August, the Charity Commission criticised trustees of the Edgware United Synagogue in London for hosting the event.

The commission said it had decided to review a recent decision to close a compliance case involving the charity.

It told MEE that "should any further concerns about the charity arise, we will consider escalating our regulatory engagement". 

Sadiq Khan says he told Met Police to investigate Great Israeli Real Estate event
Read More »

It said: "We share concerns about the potential impact, including on public trust and confidence, of registered charities being seen to actively assist in the development or expansion of illegal settlements in Palestine.

"We are also clear that charity premises must not be misused.

"Our initial compliance case found that despite their own misgivings about the event, and an organisation-wide decision to not permit it in their premises, the charity’s trustees allowed it to go ahead in one of its synagogues and did not put in place sufficient checks and controls to make sure the terms of that booking were kept."

Properties in illegal settlements advertised

Four days before the event, Middle East Eye investigation uncovered previously unreported details of the event’s connection to illegal Israeli settlements.

Emanuel Vatari, CEO of one of the sponsors of the event, the Emanuel Group, posted a list of companies participating on his Facebook page.

The list included Harey Zahav, an Israeli real estate development company whose website advertises property in Negohot, an illegal Israeli settlement in the southern Hebron Hills in the occupied West Bank.

Also on the list was The Meshulam Levinstein Group, a collection of engineering, construction and real estate companies.

It has built residential and commercial projects in illegal settlements in both the occupied West Bank and Jerusalem.

One was a housing project and a commercial centre it built in the settlement neighbourhood of Homat Shmuel in occupied East Jerusalem.

Another participant is the Tivuch Shelly real estate agency, which advertises properties in Ma'ale Adunim - a West Bank settlement.

MEE had sent evidence of the event's connections to companies involved in illegal settlements to the Foreign Office.

A Foreign Office spokesperson responded: "Israeli settlements are illegal under international law and are a fundamental threat to long-term peace and security for both Israelis and Palestinians.

"On 9 June, we updated our Business Risk Guidance to make it clear and unambiguous: if you are a British citizen or business, you should not conduct any economic and financial activities in illegal Israeli settlements.”

“The insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is the result of US actions, and if the international community is concerned about rising fuel prices, it should reprimand the United States,” Baghaei said during a televised interview on Friday.

Baghaei accused the United States of violating the Islamabad MoU only 23 days after its signing, adding the US’s “pretexts” for carrying out attacks “had no basis”.

item.description:
500 Yemeni refugees arrive in Djibouti, economy minister Ilyas Dawaleh says

Nearly 500 refugees, including women and children, from Yemen have arrived in Djibouti’s coastal city of Obock, according to the country’s minister of economy and finance, Ilyas Dawaleh.

Dawaleh wrote on X that the refugees were rescued at sea from boats stranded without fuel. 

At least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated last week, the UN’s International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Friday.

Yemeni government-run Executive Unit for the Management of Displaced Persons Camps said 1,367 families were displaced on 8 September alone in the provinces of Taiz, Al-Hudaydah and Lahj.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Lebanon president visits bombed Nabatieh site: 'No new talks with Israel'
item.description:
Lebanon president visits bombed Nabatieh site: 'No new talks with Israel'

Lebanese president Joseph Aoun visited the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh on Saturday, near a strategic Hezbollah position that the Israeli army had blown up on Thursday, and announced that there would be no new negotiations with Israel at present.

Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency said that Aoun, who was accompanied by security chiefs, “stressed that the withdrawal of Israeli forces, the return of prisoners and displaced people, and reconstruction remain national constants that Lebanon is committed to upholding”.

The visit comes a day after a US diplomatic official announced that the new round of US-brokered diplomatic talks between Israel and Lebanon, originally scheduled for next week in Rome, has been postponed until October.

Arriving without prior announcement, Aoun expressed solidarity with the residents who welcomed him, according to footage broadcast by local media.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] AI may be denting computer science graduates’ job prospects, UK data shows
item.description:
Economics graduates also appear to be affected as demand for them falls in well-paid roles in finance

AI may be warping the job prospects for students in the previously high-demand subjects of computer science and economics, according to a detailed look into the careers of recent UK graduates.

Data obtained for the 2027 Guardian University Guide published on Saturday shows that coding and software development were the fastest-falling occupations for graduates last year, while employer demand for graduates in well-paid roles in financial categories such as economists and management consultants also declined.
